--- title: "DuckDB for Marketing Analytics: From Parquet to Powerful Queries" subtitle: "How to Combine DuckDB with Arrow + Parquet" description: "This page describes DuckDB and compares it with Arrow and Parquet and explain how to use them together effectively when dealing with big data" categories: [DuckDB, Arrow, Parquet] order: 2 author: "Jae Jung" date: today format: html: theme: cosmo toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-expand: 1 code-fold: show toc-location: right-body number-sections: true #embed-resources: true execute: warning: false message: false echo: fenced cache: true freeze: auto --- # Introduction ## What is DuckDB? DuckDB is an embedded analytical database engine — think of it as "SQLite, but built for analytics." It runs entirely inside your R process with no server, no installation, no configuration. You just install the package and it works. It was designed from the ground up for **OLAP** (Online Analytical Processing) workloads — the kind of heavy aggregations, joins, and scans that are typical in data analysis, as opposed to transactional row-by-row operations. - SQLite was built for this (transactional — many small reads/writes): - "Insert one customer order" - "Update one user's address" - "Delete one session record" - DuckDB was built for this (analytical — few large scans): - "What was total revenue by channel across 50 million events?" - "Which pages had the highest bounce rate last quarter?" - "Give me the 99th percentile session duration by device type" ## Three Remarkable Features ### 1. It Lives Inside R — No Server Needed **Traditional database setup** (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake): 1. Install database server 2. Configure network/ports 3. Create users and permissions 4. Start the server process 5. Connect from R 6. Manage the server forever **DuckDB setup**: ``` install.packages("duckdb") library(duckdb) con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) # That's it. Running in 1 second. ``` ### 2. It Is Shockingly Fast > DuckDB uses columnar storage and vectorised execution — it reads only the columns your query needs and processes thousands of rows simultaneously using modern CPU instructions: **Benchmark:** Count events by type across 10 million GA4 rows - data.frame in RAM: \~4.2 seconds - data.table: \~0.8 seconds - dplyr on tibble: \~3.1 seconds - DuckDB on parquet file: \~0.3 seconds ← faster than data in RAM - DuckDB on DuckDB file: \~0.1 seconds ### 3. It Reads Parquet Directly — Without Loading Into RAM > This is the feature that changes everything for large datasets: ```{{r}} # Traditional approach — must fit in RAM ga4_data <- arrow::read_parquet("data/ga4_events.parquet") # ~4 GB into RAM result <- ga4_data |> filter(...) |> summarise(...) # then query # DuckDB approach — reads only what the query needs con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb()) result <- dbGetQuery(con, " SELECT event_name, COUNT(*) as n FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_events.parquet') WHERE event_date >= '2021-01-01' GROUP BY event_name ") # DuckDB scans only the event_name and event_date columns # Never loads price, device, geo, or any other column into RAM ``` ## Why use DuckDB? **It's fast.** DuckDB uses a columnar execution engine with vectorized query processing, meaning it processes chunks of columns at a time rather than row by row. For analytical queries on large data, this is dramatically faster than base R or even many database solutions. **It's serverless.** No Docker, no Postgres instance, no DBA needed. It lives inside your session like any other R package. **It speaks SQL fluently.** You can write standard SQL, or use it as a dplyr backend via dbplyr — so you don't need to learn a new API. **It handles larger-than-memory data.** DuckDB can query files that don't fit in RAM by streaming and processing them in chunks, making it genuinely useful for big data workflows. **It integrates natively with Parquet and Arrow.** It can directly query `.parquet` files on disk without loading them into memory first — no import step needed. ## DuckDB vs Arrow vs Parquet These three are complementary, not competing. Understanding the role of each is important: | | **Parquet** | **Arrow** | **DuckDB** | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | What is it? | File format (How data is stored on disk) | In-memory format + compute engine (a toolkit): how data is held in RAM and processed | A query engine (how you ask questions of data) | | Lives where? | Disk | RAM | RAM + disk (processes from disk) | | Primary role | Store data efficiently | Process data in memory | Query data with SQL/dplyr | | Reads Parquet | IS Parquet | Yes — natively | Yes — directly | | SQL support | No | Limited (via DuckDB) | Full SQL | | dplyr support | Via arrow package | Yes — first class" | Yes — via dbplyr | | Larger-than-memory? | Yes (it's on disk) | Partial (via chunked datasets) | Yes – streams from disk | | Query language | None | dplyr verbs | SQL + dplyr via dbplyr | | Speed (analytics) | N/A (Storage only) | Very fast | Extremely fast | | Best for | Archiving & sharing data | In-memory transformation: e.g., Wrangling in R/Python | Complex queries, joins, aggregations | The typical mental model is: - **Parquet** is where your data *lives* (on disk, compressed, efficient) - **Arrow** is how you *move and process* it quickly in memory - **DuckDB** is how you *query* it with full SQL power, with or without loading into memory They work beautifully together — DuckDB can read Arrow tables directly and query Parquet files on disk, and you can pass results back to Arrow or collect into R. # How DuckDB Works with Arrow and Parquet There are **four integration patterns**, each suited to different situations: ## Setup ```{{r}} library(duckdb) library(arrow) library(dplyr) ``` ## Pattern 1. Query a Parquet file directly with DuckDB (no loading into R) - The most direct approach — point DuckDB at a Parquet file and query it with SQL, no loading required: - DuckDB can scan Parquet files on disk using SQL — nothing enters R memory until you `collect()`. - **Simple**: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) # Register and query a parquet file directly dbGetQuery(con, " SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM read_parquet('data/sales.parquet') GROUP BY region ORDER BY total_sales DESC ") ``` ```` ::: - **Advanced**: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false library(duckdb) library(DBI) con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) # Register and query a parquet file directly dbGetQuery( con, " SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM read_parquet('data/sales.parquet') GROUP BY region ORDER BY total_sales DESC " ) # ── Query a single Parquet file ──────────────────────────────────────────────── dbGetQuery( con, " SELECT event_name, COUNT(*) AS events, COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet') GROUP BY event_name ORDER BY events DESC LIMIT 10 " ) # ── Query multiple Parquet files with a wildcard ─────────────────────────────── # Perfect for GA4's one-file-per-day structure dbGetQuery( con, " SELECT event_date, COUNT(*) AS daily_events FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_*.parquet') GROUP BY event_date ORDER BY event_date " ) dbGetQuery( con, " SELECT year, SUM(revenue) AS total FROM read_parquet('data/sales/*.parquet', union_by_name = TRUE) GROUP BY year ORDER BY year " # ── Join two Parquet files in a single query ─────────────────────────────────── dbGetQuery( con, " SELECT s.device_category, s.traffic_source_medium, COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_pseudo_id) AS users, SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchases FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet') AS e JOIN read_parquet('data/ga4_sessions.parquet') AS s ON e.user_pseudo_id = s.user_pseudo_id AND e.event_date = s.event_date GROUP BY s.device_category, s.traffic_source_medium ORDER BY users DESC " ) dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) ``` ```` ::: This is powerful — DuckDB pushes the entire query down to the file, reading only the columns and rows it needs (thanks to Parquet's columnar layout). ## Parttern 2. Use DuckDB as a dplyr backend (no SQL required) > If you prefer dplyr verbs over SQL, you can register the **Parquet file** as a **virtual table** and query it lazily. > `dbplyr` translates dplyr verbs into DuckDB SQL automatically: - **Simple**: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) duckdb_register(con, "sales", read_parquet("data/sales.parquet")) tbl(con, "sales") |> filter(year >= 2022) |> group_by(region) |> summarise(total = sum(sales)) |> arrange(desc(total)) |> collect() # only now does data enter R ``` ```` ::: - **Advanced**: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false library(duckdb) library(dplyr) library(dbplyr) library(DBI) con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) # ── Register Parquet file as a virtual table ─────────────────────────────────── # This creates a view — no data is copied or loaded duckdb_read_csv # (there is also this for CSV) dbExecute(con, " CREATE VIEW ga4_events AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet') ") dbExecute(con, " CREATE VIEW ga4_sessions AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_sessions.parquet') ") # ── Now use dplyr as if it were a regular data frame ────────────────────────── events <- tbl(con, "ga4_events") sessions <- tbl(con, "ga4_sessions") # dplyr query — translated to DuckDB SQL by dbplyr top_events <- events |> count(event_name, sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> collect() # collect() executes the query and returns a tibble print(top_events) # Join two Parquet files using dplyr — no SQL written device_conversions <- sessions |> select(user_pseudo_id, device_category, traffic_source_medium) |> left_join( events |> filter(event_name == "purchase") |> distinct(user_pseudo_id) |> mutate(purchased = TRUE), by = "user_pseudo_id" ) |> mutate(purchased = coalesce(purchased, FALSE)) |> group_by(device_category, traffic_source_medium) |> summarise( users = n_distinct(user_pseudo_id), purchasers = sum(as.integer(purchased), na.rm = TRUE), cvr = purchasers / users, .groups = "drop" ) |> arrange(desc(cvr)) |> collect() # only now does data enter R print(device_conversions) dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) ``` ```` ::: ## Pattern 3. Query an Arrow Table with DuckDB (The Power Combination) > Arrow and DuckDB are designed to work together. Arrow handles file I/O and in-memory transformation; DuckDB handles querying. > They share data without copying, using the Apache Arrow memory format. > If you already have an Arrow table in memory, DuckDB can query it directly — zero copying involved: - **Simple**: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false # Create or load an Arrow table arrow_table <- read_parquet("data/sales.parquet", as_data_frame = FALSE) con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) duckdb_register_arrow(con, "sales_arrow", arrow_table) tbl(con, "sales_arrow") |> filter(category == "Electronics") |> summarise(avg_price = mean(price)) |> collect() ``` ```` ::: - **Advanced**: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false library(arrow) library(duckdb) library(dplyr) # ── Step 1: Open Parquet as Arrow Dataset (lazy — nothing loaded yet) ────────── ga4_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet") # ── Step 2: Do transformations in Arrow ─────────────────────────────────────── # Arrow is better at: filtering rows, selecting columns, type conversion ga4_prepared <- ga4_arrow |> filter(event_name %in% c("purchase", "add_to_cart", "view_item")) |> select(event_date, event_name, user_pseudo_id) |> mutate(event_date = as.Date(event_date)) # ── Step 3: Hand off to DuckDB for aggregation ──────────────────────────────── # DuckDB is better at: GROUP BY, window functions, complex joins con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) # Register the Arrow object directly — ZERO data copying duckdb_register_arrow(con, "ga4_prepared", ga4_prepared) # Now query it with full DuckDB SQL power result <- dbGetQuery(con, " SELECT event_date, event_name, COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users FROM ga4_prepared GROUP BY event_date, event_name ORDER BY event_date, event_name ") print(result) dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) # ── The same workflow using dplyr throughout ─────────────────────────────────── library(arrow) library(duckdb) library(dplyr) con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb()) # Arrow dataset → register with DuckDB → query with dplyr ga4_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_flat.parquet") duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "ga4_events", ga4_arrow) ga4_params_arrow <- arrow::open_dataset("data/ga4_event_params.parquet") duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(con, "ga4_params", ga4_params_arrow) # Now use pure dplyr — no SQL needed at all # dbplyr translates these verbs to DuckDB SQL automatically # Marketing analysis: page views by device and channel page_analysis <- tbl(con, "ga4_params") |> filter(key == "page_location") |> rename(page_location = param_value) |> left_join( tbl(con, "ga4_events") |> select(event_timestamp, user_pseudo_id, device_category, traffic_source_medium), by = c("event_timestamp", "user_pseudo_id") ) |> mutate( page_path = regexp_replace(page_location, "\\?.*$", ""), page_path = regexp_replace(page_path, "https?://[^/]+", "") ) |> group_by(device_category, page_path) |> summarise( page_views = n(), users = n_distinct(user_pseudo_id), .groups = "drop" ) |> filter(page_views >= 10) |> arrange(desc(page_views)) |> head(20) |> collect() print(page_analysis) dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) ``` ```` ::: ## Pattern 4. Persistent DuckDB Database (Best for a Course Project) > Write your rectangled GA4 tables once into a `.duckdb` file. Every subsequent analysis opens this one file — no BigQuery, no Parquet management, no RAM issues: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false library(duckdb) library(dplyr) library(arrow) # ── SETUP: Run once to create the database ──────────────────────────────────── con <- dbConnect( duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = "data/ga4.duckdb", read_only = FALSE ) # Write tables from Parquet files — DuckDB reads and stores them dbExecute(con, " CREATE TABLE ga4_events AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_flat.parquet') ") dbExecute(con, " CREATE TABLE ga4_params AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_event_params.parquet') ") dbExecute(con, " CREATE TABLE ga4_sessions AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_sessions.parquet') ") dbExecute(con, " CREATE TABLE ga4_items AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('data/ga4_items.parquet') ") # Add indexes for faster querying dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_event_name ON ga4_events(event_name)") dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_param_key ON ga4_params(key)") dbExecute(con, "CREATE INDEX idx_event_date ON ga4_events(event_date)") # Confirm what was saved cat("Tables in ga4.duckdb:\n") dbListTables(con) |> print() cat("\nRow counts:\n") purrr::map_df(dbListTables(con), \(t) { tibble::tibble( table = t, rows = dbGetQuery(con, glue::glue("SELECT COUNT(*) n FROM {t}"))$n ) }) |> print() cat("\nFile size:", round(file.size("data/ga4.duckdb") / 1024^2, 1), "MB\n") dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) ``` ```` ::: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false # ── ANALYSIS: Open the database for every subsequent session ────────────────── con <- dbConnect( duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = "data/ga4.duckdb", read_only = TRUE # Prevents accidental writes during analysis ) # Lazy table references — nothing in RAM yet events <- tbl(con, "ga4_events") params <- tbl(con, "ga4_params") sessions <- tbl(con, "ga4_sessions") items <- tbl(con, "ga4_items") # ── Example 1: Event counts (dplyr) ─────────────────────────────────────────── events |> count(event_name, sort = TRUE) |> collect() # ── Example 2: Top pages (dplyr) ────────────────────────────────────────────── params |> filter(key == "page_location") |> count(param_value, sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> collect() # ── Example 3: Revenue by day (SQL) ─────────────────────────────────────────── dbGetQuery(con, " SELECT event_date, COUNT(*) AS transactions, SUM(ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd) AS revenue, AVG(ecommerce_purchase_revenue_in_usd) AS avg_order_value FROM ga4_events WHERE event_name = 'purchase' GROUP BY event_date ORDER BY event_date ") # ── Example 4: Funnel analysis (SQL window functions) ───────────────────────── dbGetQuery(con, " WITH funnel AS ( SELECT event_name, COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS users, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ( ORDER BY CASE event_name WHEN 'view_item' THEN 1 WHEN 'add_to_cart' THEN 2 WHEN 'begin_checkout' THEN 3 WHEN 'purchase' THEN 4 END ) AS stage_order FROM ga4_events WHERE event_name IN ('view_item','add_to_cart', 'begin_checkout','purchase') GROUP BY event_name ) SELECT event_name, users, ROUND(100.0 * users / FIRST_VALUE(users) OVER (ORDER BY stage_order), 1) AS pct_of_top FROM funnel ORDER BY stage_order ") dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) ``` ```` ::: # How the Three Tools Form a Complete Stack ``` # The complete GA4 analytics stack: # ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ # │ YOUR R SESSION │ # │ │ # │ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ # │ │ Arrow │ │ dplyr │ │ ggplot2 │ │ # │ │ │ │ dbplyr │ │ gt │ │ # │ │ Read & │ │ │ │ │ │ # │ │ Write │ │ Verbs → │ │ Visualise & Report │ │ # │ │ Parquet │ │ SQL │ │ │ │ # │ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └───────────┬──────────┘ │ # │ │ │ │ │ # │ └───────────────▼───────────────────────┘ │ # │ ┌──────────┐ │ # │ │ DuckDB │ │ # │ │ │ │ # │ │ Query │ │ # │ │ Engine │ │ # │ └────┬─────┘ │ # └───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┘ # │ # ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ # │ │ │ # ┌─────▼──────┐ ┌─────▼──────┐ ┌───▼────────────┐ # │ Parquet │ │ Parquet │ │ ga4.duckdb │ # │ ga4_flat │ │ ga4_params│ │ (all tables) │ # └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘ # DISK DISK DISK # Arrow = the loading dock (moves data efficiently) # DuckDB = the analyst (asks and answers questions) # Parquet = the filing system (stores data efficiently) ``` # The Big Picture Workflow ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **Parquet is your warehouse, Arrow is your forklift, DuckDB is your analyst.** Each does its job, and they hand off to each other seamlessly.
